items.title: Exploring Pre-training Benefits on Phoneme Addition through Fine-tuning in Speech Synthesis
items.authors: Masato Murata(CyberAgent; Nagoya University); Koichi Miyazaki(CyberAgent); Tomoki Koriyama(CyberAgent); Tomoki Toda(Nagoya University)
items.abstract: Transfer learning is widely used for low-resource text-to-speech. When the target corpus contains phonemes unseen in pre-training, the model must expand its phoneme inventory during fine-tuning; we call the process "phoneme addition." However, it remains unclear whether the pre-trained ability to generate seen phonemes contributes to this process. This study investigates phoneme addition in two settings: (1) a simulation setup using LLM-generated phoneme-controlled corpora that enables investigation without considering confounding factors, and (2) a real-speech cross-lingual transfer setup (English to Japanese) to validate whether the findings hold in practice. Experiments in both settings showed that while fine-tuning achieved higher naturalness than training from scratch, it required as much or more data to achieve comparable PER for new phonemes. These results indicate that pre-training mainly contributes to naturalness improvement, but offers limited benefit for phoneme addition.

items.title: ES-3DF: Editable Speech-Driven 3D Face Reconstruction via Geometry Texture Disentanglement
items.authors: Jianrong Wang(Tianjin University; Tianjin Renai College); Kaibin Bi(Tianjin University); Jinghui Li(Tianjin Renai College); Ju Zhang(Tianjin University of Technology); Qi Li(Tianjin University); Ying Guo(Tianjin University); Jing Zhao(Tianjin Beiyang Rongke Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd.)
items.abstract: Speech-driven facial generation typically relies on 2D synthesis, limiting realism and applicability. We propose ES-3DF, the first framework to reconstruct editable, textured 3D faces directly from speech. ES-3DF employs a Disentangle module that decouples facial features into 3DMM geometry and UV texture maps to enable fine-grained editing. To bridge the modality gap, we introduce a Dual-Branch Alignment module enhanced by a Class-Aware Multi-Slot Memory Bank. By leveraging a novel Multi-Slot InfoNCE loss, this mechanism dynamically aligns speech embeddings with diverse, evolving speaker prototypes, significantly improving identity preservation in the latent space. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ES-3DF outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in geometric accuracy, identity preservation, and visual quality, underscoring its potential for realistic 3D avatar generation.

items.title: K-DIALECT : Korean Dialect-Aware Face-Based Speech Synthesis
items.authors: Seongyeon Yang(Sungkyunkwan University); Juyeob Lee(Sungkyunkwan University); Eunil Park(Sungkyunkwan University; Jaume I University)
items.abstract: Korean exhibits substantial regional variation, comprising five major dialects in addition to the standard Seoul dialect. These dialects convey distinctive prosodic patterns and reflect important aspects of cultural and speaker identities. However, most Text-to-Speech (TTS) systems are primarily designed for standard language, limiting their ability to represent dialectal characteristics, particularly in low-resource dialect settings. Although face-based speech synthesis provides a viable alternative when reference audio is scarce or noisy, modeling dialectal prosody within this paradigm remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we propose K-DIALECT, a multimodal face-based TTS framework for synthesizing low-resource Korean dialects. The model integrates a face encoder, a dialect-conditioned pitch predictor, and a FiLM-based fusion module. Experiments on six Korean dialects demonstrate improvements in dialectal fluency, naturalness, and modality alignment.

items.title: Feature Design and Generative Modelling in Deep Articulatory Synthesis
items.authors: Charles McGhee(University of Cambridge); Mark J.F. Gales(University of Cambridge); Kate M. Knill(University of Cambridge)
items.abstract: A deep articulatory synthesiser learns a mapping from a set of articulatory features to a set of acoustic features. A growing use case of articulatory synthesis is as an evaluation method for articulatory inversion, the process of estimating articulation from speech. To complete the loop from speech to articulation to speech, information lost during inversion must be added back in to faithfully recreate the input speech. This information can be added explicitly via additional input features or implicitly through generative modelling. However, by adding this information back into the synthesis process, the resulting speech may not be representative of the articulation estimated from inversion. In this work, we explore the impact of different feature inputs and modelling types on the output of a synthesiser, demonstrating that careful design choices are required to make claims about articulation through synthesis results.

items.title: From Tokens to Faces: Investigating Discrete Speech Representations for 3D Facial Animation
items.authors: Pedro R. Corrêa(UNICAMP; Univ. Grenoble Alpes, CNRS, Grenoble INP, GIPSA-lab); Olivier Perrotin(Univ. Grenoble Alpes, CNRS, Grenoble INP, GIPSA-lab); Samir Sadok(Inria at Univ. Grenoble Alpes); Paula D. P. Costa(UNICAMP); Thomas Hueber(Univ. Grenoble Alpes, CNRS, Grenoble INP, GIPSA-lab)
items.abstract: The choice of speech representation is critical in speech-driven 3D facial animation. Representations differ in what they encode: SSL features emphasize segmental and semantic cues, neural codecs yield latents optimized for acoustic reconstruction, and ASR-style objectives produce label-based spaces. We evaluate four speech representation families for 3D facial synthesis, comparing their facial reconstruction quality across two facial decoders using objective metrics and a perceptual evaluation. We additionally conduct probing analyses that relate tokenized representations to phonetic units and to articulatory deformations. We found that encoding phonetic classes is beneficial for accurate facial animation prediction on both semantic and label-based representations with comparable facial animation quality. From the latter, we introduce an Audio Visual Text-to-Speech (AVTTS) pipeline that leverages, as a shared space, discrete representations to decode speech and 3D facial motion.

items.title: Not Quite My Tempo: Voice Activity-aware Speech Synthesis for Lip-Synchronous Dubbing
items.authors: Alejandro Pérez-González-de-Martos(AppTek GmbH); Florian Lux(AppTek GmbH); Angelina Elizarova(AppTek GmbH); Milana Shkhanukova(AppTek GmbH); Andreas Kellner(AppTek GmbH); Mattia Antonino Di Gangi(AppTek GmbH)
items.abstract: Automatic lip-synchronous dubbing requires a speech synthesis model to generate alternating voice and silence patterns in the target language that match the timing of the source clip precisely to ensure an optimal viewing experience. Prior works address this problem by conditioning the speech synthesis process on lip movements extracted from the video signal. In this work, we condition the speech generation on a binary voice-activity signal, which has a lightweight representation and can be produced in multiple ways. We show that the model follows the voice-activity signal with high accuracy while maintaining natural prosody and semantically appropriate pause placement within sentences, as demonstrated through extensive objective and subjective evaluations. By randomly masking this condition during training, we make the feature entirely optional during inference, allowing editors to enforce or relax lip-sync constraints when desired.

items.title: GETS: Guiding EMG-to-Speech Synthesis via Silent Speech Recognition
items.authors: Jiwon Lee(Seoul National University); Jaejun Lee(Seoul National University); Kyogu Lee(Seoul National University)
items.abstract: Electromyography-to-speech (ETS) offers a promising solution for voicing silent speech, yet conventional methods often struggle to achieve high semantic intelligibility. We introduce GETS, a novel framework that establishes a new state-of-the-art (SOTA) with a Word Error Rate (WER) of 11.89% on the silent EMG test set. GETS comprises a diffusion-based generative network conditioned on EMG signals, integrated with a semantic guidance mechanism derived from silent speech recognition (SSR). Our framework not only demonstrates superior semantic intelligibility by effectively disambiguating underspecified EMG inputs but also faithfully preserves the prosodic characteristics--such as temporal alignment and energy contours--inherent in the original EMG signals. This synergistic fusion of acoustic EMG cues and SSR-based semantic guidance establishes a new benchmark for high-fidelity, naturalistic silent speech communication.

items.title: Enhancing EMG-to-Speech via Silent-Voiced Representation Alignment
items.authors: Jiwon Lee(Seoul National University); Injune Hwang(Seoul National University); Jaejun Lee(Seoul National University); Eungbeom Kim(Seoul National University); Dongyub Han(Seoul National University); Kyogu Lee(Seoul National University)
items.abstract: Silent Speech Interfaces (SSIs) offer an alternative communication pathway by reconstructing intelligible speech from non-acoustic biosignals such as facial electromyography (EMG). In particular, EMG can capture muscle activity associated with articulatory movements even in the absence of vocalization, serving as a suitable modality for silent speech synthesis. A major challenge in EMG-to-speech (ETS) research is the natural absence of ground-truth speech for silent EMG, along with the scarcity of available data. To address this, we propose a novel Silent-Voiced Alignment (SVA) loss, which introduces a multi-level representation-based alignment objective between utterance-parallel silent and voiced EMG pairs. Extensive experiments show that our method significantly enhances content reconstruction and can be seamlessly integrated into existing ETS frameworks. Furthermore, we demonstrate enhanced intelligibility and robustness under a standardized evaluation protocol.

items.title: Automatic pitch prediction from speech articulation: Where does the f0 information come from?
items.authors: Beliz Ozkan(Université Grenoble Alpes); Jonas Michael(Université Grenoble Alpes); Thomas Hueber(Université Grenoble Alpes); Olivier Perrotin(Université Grenoble Alpes)
items.abstract: While source-filter theory posits independence between the glottal source and vocal tract, empirical studies on silent speech interfaces predict fo from articulatory data. Using a multi-speaker dataset, we found that ultrasound tongue images alone do enable partial fo prediction. To resolve this paradox, we tested four hypotheses. We found no evidence that fo prediction (1) relies on a specific structure other than the tongue (or lips); (2) benefits from increased temporal context. However, (3) models trained on isolated utterances failed to generalise to spontaneous speech. Most importantly, (4) prominent words were predicted more accurately by capturing local correlations between fo and articulatory dynamics. These findings, corroborated by a perceptive experiment, highlight the need for realistic conversational training data and a focus on predicting local prosodic functions—rather than replicating global fo trajectories—to better capture the pragmatic role of fo in communication.

items.title: Speaker-Independent Speech Synthesis from Real-time MRI Articulatory Data
items.authors: Yuto Otani(Tokyo University of Science); Shun Sawada(Nippon Institute of Technology); Hidefumi Ohmura(Tokyo University of Science); Kouichi Katsurada(Tokyo University of Science)
items.abstract: This paper proposes a speaker-independent speech synthesis method that generates speech waveforms from real-time MRI (rtMRI) videos. The proposed model uses EfficientNetV2 for per-frame feature extraction, E-Branchformer for temporal modeling, and BigVGAN-v2 for speech synthesis. Speaker characteristics are acquired from rtMRI videos through cross-modal training with speaker embeddings, enabling speaker-independent synthesis from rtMRI videos alone. Experiments using the USC 75-Speaker Speech MRI Database demonstrate that the proposed method achieves favorable linguistic accuracy for read speech in a speaker-independent setting. F0 correlation analysis indicates that relative prosodic patterns are captured to a reasonable extent, as expected from visual articulatory information, though absolute F0 estimation remains challenging. Speaker similarity results show that although within-gender speaker discrimination proved difficult, speaker identity is reproduced to a reasonable degree.
